content: Congenital syphilis is a severe condition that results in fetal or perinatal death in approximately 40% of affected infants. This disease, first described in the 15th century, has long been recognized as a distinct syndrome caused by transmission of infection from an infected adult. Various theories have been proposed to explain its transmission, including paternal transmission and transmission through an infected wet nurse. However, transplacental transmission from an asymptomatic infected mother was first documented in 1906. Despite the availability of penicillin treatment for syphilis during pregnancy, congenital syphilis has not been eradicated. Since the 1970s, the incidence of congenital syphilis has closely mirrored the rates of primary and secondary syphilis in women. In 1986, the number of reported cases of congenital syphilis in the United States reached a 15-year high, with 365 cases reported to the CDC. That year, nearly one in every 10,000 live-born infants in the U.S. was affected by congenital syphilis. The proportion of stillbirths caused by syphilis remains unknown. In July 1987, the CDC convened a group of 10 consultants to address the problem of congenital syphilis and develop potential solutions. The resulting guidelines, published as a supplement to the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR), aim to provide focused and coordinated guidance for healthcare providers. Although some aspects of these guidelines are based on limited data, they represent the best judgment of experts in the field. Surveillance of congenital syphilis should be conducted at local, state, and national levels. The provisional case definition includes any infant under 12 months of age with one of the following: a reactive non-treponemal serologic test for syphilis confirmed by a reactive treponemal test, a positive darkfield microscopic examination of a non-oral mucous membrane, or a positive fluorescent antibody test for Treponema pallidum on any lesion. Physicians, clinics, and hospitals are required to report all cases meeting this definition to local public health authorities. Laboratories must also report indicative findings. Areas with five or more women with early infectious syphilis per 100,000 population should establish active surveillance systems for congenital syphilis at key hospitals. Hospitals in high-incidence areas or those serving at-risk populations should routinely perform serologic tests for syphilis (STS) using umbilical cord blood samples. Cases classified as confirmed, compatible, or requiring additional information should be reported to state public health authorities. These reports help identify problem areas and ensure appropriate follow-up at the state level. Surveillance information is used to determine the reasons for specific cases and to identify trends. Investigators should complete these forms by the time an infant reaches eight months of age, even for cases lost to follow-up. Confirmed cases of congenital syphilis involve the identification of T. pallidum through darkfield microscopy, fluorescent antibody testing, or other specific stains in specimens from lesions, autopsy material, placenta, or umbilical cord. Alternatively, a live-born infant without symptoms whose mother was treated for syphilis during pregnancy and demonstrated a fourfold or greater fall in titer, with the infant's STS also being fourfold or lower than the maternal titer at the time of treatment, may also be classified as a confirmed case. Surveillance systems for congenital syphilis require sensitivity to ensure that state and local sexually transmitted disease (STD) control programs are aware of reactive STS results. These programs should evaluate and follow individual reactive serologic test reports and monitor laboratory and clinician reporting patterns. A quality assurance system is necessary to confirm that all medical laboratories performing STD tests comply with official reporting regulations. Compliance should be checked regularly, at least every six months, through letters, phone calls, or personal visits. State health departments should maintain a central registry of patients treated for syphilis, including detailed information about the stage of disease, type and amount of medication administered, laboratory test results, and, if the patient is pregnant, the trimester during which treatment occurred. This information is critical for the proper medical management of pregnant women, their fetuses, and their infants. Strict confidentiality and data security procedures must be established, periodically reviewed, and independently tested to prevent misuse or unauthorized disclosure of registry information. Controlling early infectious syphilis is essential for preventing congenital syphilis. When the prevalence of infectious syphilis increases significantly among women of reproductive age, cases of congenital syphilis are likely to follow. Recent years have seen increased prevalence in several areas of the United States. To prevent future cases, STD control programs must emphasize early syphilis control, particularly in high-incidence areas. Traditional tools for early syphilis control include patient interviews to identify sexual partners, rapid partner notification, selective re-interviews, and clustering around the patient and their examined sexual partners to identify others at risk of infection. Recommended techniques and procedures are discussed in disease intervention courses sponsored by the Division of Sexually Transmitted Diseases. Specific activities for state and local STD control programs to prevent congenital syphilis include ensuring that public health statutes mandate STS testing for all pregnant women during their initial prenatal visit and early in the third trimester. Public and private laboratories should be monitored regularly to ensure prompt and thorough reporting of reactive STS results. The pregnancy status of women diagnosed with syphilis and the partners of men with syphilis should be assessed. Women in high-incidence neighborhoods who may be pregnant should be identified and referred for serologic testing and prenatal care. All women of reproductive age seen in STD clinics should be informed about the need for prenatal care and STS testing in future pregnancies. Prenatal screening for syphilis should be encouraged wherever pregnant women receive healthcare, including WIC programs, methadone clinics, detention facilities, and prenatal care facilities. Educational messages should be delivered to the medical community about laboratory tests, diagnostic criteria, treatment, and follow-up for at-risk patients. Public service educational messages should target women who share demographic characteristics with those most often diagnosed with early syphilis, such as young, single, minority women living in central city neighborhoods.
